turns.text:
I couldn't get live prices for Dec 6–13. The SUV card shows Kayak's typical rates, and a mid-size like the Blazer or Escape runs about $36–37/day, so roughly $260 for the week before taxes and fees. December is peak season, so check your exact dates on Kayak. Alamo has the best reviews among the major agencies at OGG.

For snorkel gear, Amazon was the best value at $36.98 for two sets, and Walmart blocked me. The Aegend set ($26.99, 4.9★) is the top-rated full set with fins. If you only need a mask and snorkel, the Kwambiri ($10.99) or Wutrye ($15.99) are cheaper. Rental fins are easy to find on Maui, so a dry-top mask and snorkel may be enough.

I found several Marriott-family hotels under your budget for Dec 10–13. Prices come back in USD, and all of them are under €400 a night. I didn't see any Hyatt in the results.

- **Best pick for location:** Renaissance Paris République ($265/night, 4.5★). It's a 5-star Marriott hotel, but it's a bit farther from the Louvre than the others.
- **Best value:** Clubtrotteur Paris, a Tribute Portfolio hotel, at $160/night. It has a 4.9 rating, but only 21 reviews.
- **Closest to the Louvre area:** Paris Marriott Opera Ambassador at $386/night. It's near your cap and has a 4.1 rating.
- **Cheapest big-name option:** Paris Marriott Rive Gauche at $168/night. It's on the Left Bank, not next to the Louvre.

The Courtyard Gare de Lyon is $206/night but is also not near the Louvre. The stays card has the listings and booking links.

turns.text:
I made a 15-song 80s road-trip playlist. It starts with driving anthems like Tom Petty and Van Halen, then moves to sing-alongs like Journey and Bon Jovi. It finishes with synth-pop and Toto's "Africa". Tap any card to open the song in Apple Music, then add them to a playlist there.

Most songs are the original 80s recordings. "Runnin' Down a Dream" is the 1989 greatest-hits version, and "Under Pressure" is a 2017 remaster of the 1981 single.

Home
Blog
Palo Alto Heat Pump Rebates: The Complete CPAU Guide

BLOG / REBATES
What CPAU pays when you replace a gas heater with a heat pump, which add-ons stack, and the 90-day deadline people miss.By the ComfortFlow teamUpdated October 11, 20265 min read
Call 650-460-3483

City of Palo Alto Utilities offers a Heat Pump HVAC rebate of $2,500, or $5,000 for income-eligible residents, when a heat pump replaces a gas or fossil fuel heater. Add-on rebates cover a qualifying panel upgrade ($1,000, or $2,000 income-eligible) and $500 per qualifying circuit or device. Applications are due within 90 days of final inspection.
Who qualifies
The CPAU Heat Pump HVAC rebate is for City of Palo Alto Utilities residential customers. The key rule is simple: the new heat pump must replace a gas or fossil fuel home heater. Replacing an existing electric heat pump or adding cooling to a home that already heats electrically doesn’t qualify for the core rebate.
If you live in Menlo Park, East Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos or on the Stanford campus, you aren’t a CPAU customer, and different programs apply. See our service area pages for notes on each.
Rebate amounts (as published on the City of Palo Alto Rebate Hub)
RebateStandardIncome-eligibleKey rule
Heat Pump HVAC (core)$2,500$5,000Must replace a gas or fossil fuel heater
Electrical panel upgrade (add-on)$1,000$2,000Paired with a core rebate; new panel 200 amps or less
Panel upgrade permit fee (add-on)Not offered$1,000Income-eligible only
Prewiring, circuit splitter/pauser, subpanel (add-on)$500 each$500 eachMust serve the new heat pump; limits apply

Rebates change. We confirm the current numbers with CPAU before you sign a contract.
How add-ons work
Add-on rebates are not available for standalone projects. They must be paired with a core rebate like Heat Pump HVAC. The wiring add-on is limited to one subpanel rebate and two circuit splitter or pauser rebates per household. If you also replace a gas water heater with a heat pump water heater, that has its own core rebate and separate application.
The steps
Get an assessment. We confirm the existing heater is gas, check the panel, and design the system.
Permit. Most single-family heat pump projects can use the City’s instant permit.
Install and inspect. The project must pass final inspection.
Apply within 90 days of final inspection. This is the deadline people miss most often.

Instant rebates at the point of sale
CPAU lets you receive the rebate at the point of sale when you use a contractor listed as a CPAU Instant Rebate Partner in the City’s Contractor Directory. That means the rebate comes off your invoice instead of arriving later. Ask any contractor whether they participate.
Tips to get the most out of it
Plan the panel early. If your panel needs work, pairing it with the heat pump unlocks the add-on rebate.
Consider load management first. A circuit splitter or pauser may avoid a panel upgrade entirely, and it has its own add-on rebate.
Do the water heater too. Combining a heat pump water heater with a heat pump HVAC project can mean two core rebates and one round of electrical work.
Keep paperwork. Save the permit, final inspection record, invoice and equipment specs.

Ready to plan yours? See heat pump installation in Palo Alto or call us at 650-460-3483.
Example: how the rebates can stack
Here is how a typical Palo Alto project might combine incentives, using the amounts published on the City of Palo Alto Rebate Hub. A homeowner replaces an aging gas furnace and central air conditioner with a ducted heat pump. The project qualifies for the $2,500 Heat Pump HVAC rebate. Their 100-amp panel is tight on capacity, so they add a circuit splitter instead of upgrading the whole panel, which qualifies for a $500 add-on rebate. If the same household also replaces a gas water heater with a heat pump water heater, that is a separate core rebate with its own application.

HOME HEATING · PALO ALTO, CA · OCTOBER 2026

Choose the heat pump, unless your furnace and AC are both healthy

In Palo Alto's mild climate, with city-run electricity and rising gas rates, a heat pump is the better long-term pick. A $2,500 city rebate narrows the upfront gap.

Verdict: heat pump. You get heating and cooling in one system and a CPAU rebate of $2,500 or more. Gas rates are rising faster than electric (9% vs 4.5% in July 2026). Bay Area rules will push furnace replacements toward zero-NOx equipment from 2029. Keep a working furnace only if it is young and you don't need AC.
$2,500CPAU rebate, standard (replacing a gas heater)
$0Federal tax credit (25C ended Dec 31, 2025)
~300%Heat pump efficiency vs ≤98% for gas
+9%Palo Alto gas rate rise, July 2026

Part 1

Upfront cost

ItemGas furnaceHeat pump
Installed cost (Bay Area)$3,500–$7,500 (80% to 98% AFUE)$5,000–$12,000 per one source; $9,000–$18,000 for ducted systems per another
Cooling included?No, add an AC (extra cost)Yes
CPAU rebateNone$2,500 ($5,000 if income-eligible)
Possible panel workRarelySometimes. Panel add-on rebate: $1,000 ($2,000 income-eligible)

The gap shrinks if you would otherwise replace the AC too. One source puts the furnace+AC vs heat pump difference at $2,000–$5,000. Installer quotes vary a lot, so get three, with at least one from a CPAU Instant Rebate Partner.

Part 2

Efficiency and running cost

Delivered heat per unit of energy in (best case)

High-efficiency furnaceup to 98%
80% AFUE furnace80%
  • Palo Alto winters are mild, so heat pumps run in their efficient range nearly all season.
  • The city's median gas bill is about $78/month and electric about $89 (FY2026, before the July increases).
  • The city's own typical-customer figures are 51 therms/month in winter and 17 in summer. That implies roughly 200 therms a year of heating, my estimate. A heat pump would need around a third of that energy.
I did not find CPAU's per-kWh and per-therm rates, so I can't give an exact annual savings figure. Statewide PG&E sources say running costs are about equal at standard rates. CPAU's electricity is cheaper than PG&E's, and its gas is rising faster, so expect the heat pump to be equal or cheaper to run here. Check this against your own bills.

Part 3

Incentives (as of Oct 2026)

ProgramStatusAmount
CPAU Heat Pump HVAC rebateOpen$2,500 / $5,000 income-eligible. Must replace a gas heater.
CPAU panel upgrade add-onOpen$1,000 / $2,000 income-eligible

Rules: you must be a CPAU customer with active electric and gas accounts. Add-ons require a core rebate. Apply within 90 days of final inspection. A CPAU Instant Rebate Partner takes the rebate off your invoice. Reserve funds before installing.

Part 4

Side by side

Heat pump: pros

  • Heating and cooling in one unit
  • 2–4× more efficient than gas
  • Local rebates of $2,500 or more, plus add-ons
  • Carbon-neutral CPAU electricity
  • Not affected by the 2029 BAAQMD zero-NOx furnace rule
  • Buyers increasingly want all-electric homes

Heat pump: cons

  • Higher upfront cost
  • May need a panel upgrade or load management
  • Gentler 90–110°F air feels less "toasty" than a furnace's 120–140°F
  • No federal credit anymore

Furnace: pros

  • Cheapest to install ($3,500–$7,500)
  • No electrical upgrades
  • No mandate to remove a working furnace

Furnace: cons

  • Gas rates are up 9% in a year, with more increases projected
  • No cooling, so you still need an AC
  • Zero-NOx rule for new furnaces from 2029 (Bay Area)
  • No CPAU rebate

Next steps

How to do it

  1. Check the age of your furnace and AC. Replace both together if either is over about 12–15 years old.
  2. Get a load calculation, panel check, and duct inspection. Ask whether a circuit splitter can avoid a panel upgrade.
  3. Get 3 quotes. Ask each whether they are a CPAU Instant Rebate Partner.
  4. Reserve the rebate in the City's Rebate Hub before installing.

Palo Alto Heat Pump Rebates: The Complete CPAU Guide

BLOG / REBATES
What CPAU pays when you replace a gas heater with a heat pump, which add-ons stack, and the 90-day deadline people miss.By the ComfortFlow teamUpdated October 11, 20265 min read
Call 650-460-3483

City of Palo Alto Utilities offers a Heat Pump HVAC rebate of $2,500, or $5,000 for income-eligible residents, when a heat pump replaces a gas or fossil fuel heater. Add-on rebates cover a qualifying panel upgrade ($1,000, or $2,000 income-eligible) and $500 per qualifying circuit or device. Applications are due within 90 days of final inspection.
Who qualifies
The CPAU Heat Pump HVAC rebate is for City of Palo Alto Utilities residential customers. The key rule is simple: the new heat pump must replace a gas or fossil fuel home heater. Replacing an existing electric heat pump or adding cooling to a home that already heats electrically doesn’t qualify for the core rebate.
If you live in Menlo Park, East Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos or on the Stanford campus, you aren’t a CPAU customer, and different programs apply. See our service area pages for notes on each.
Rebate amounts (as published on the City of Palo Alto Rebate Hub)
RebateStandardIncome-eligibleKey rule
Heat Pump HVAC (core)$2,500$5,000Must replace a gas or fossil fuel heater
Electrical panel upgrade (add-on)$1,000$2,000Paired with a core rebate; new panel 200 amps or less
Panel upgrade permit fee (add-on)Not offered$1,000Income-eligible only
Prewiring, circuit splitter/pauser, subpanel (add-on)$500 each$500 eachMust serve the new heat pump; limits apply

Rebates change. We confirm the current numbers with CPAU before you sign a contract.
How add-ons work
Add-on rebates are not available for standalone projects. They must be paired with a core rebate like Heat Pump HVAC. The wiring add-on is limited to one subpanel rebate and two circuit splitter or pauser rebates per household. If you also replace a gas water heater with a heat pump water heater, that has its own core rebate and separate application.
The steps
Get an assessment. We confirm the existing heater is gas, check the panel, and design the system.
Permit. Most single-family heat pump projects can use the City’s instant permit.
Install and inspect. The project must pass final inspection.
Apply within 90 days of final inspection. This is the deadline people miss most often.

Instant rebates at the point of sale
CPAU lets you receive the rebate at the point of sale when you use a contractor listed as a CPAU Instant Rebate Partner in the City’s Contractor Directory. That means the rebate comes off your invoice instead of arriving later. Ask any contractor whether they participate.
Tips to get the most out of it
Plan the panel early. If your panel needs work, pairing it with the heat pump unlocks the add-on rebate.
Consider load management first. A circuit splitter or pauser may avoid a panel upgrade entirely, and it has its own add-on rebate.
Do the water heater too. Combining a heat pump water heater with a heat pump HVAC project can mean two core rebates and one round of electrical work.
Keep paperwork. Save the permit, final inspection record, invoice and equipment specs.

Ready to plan yours? See heat pump installation in Palo Alto or call us at 650-460-3483.
Example: how the rebates can stack
Here is how a typical Palo Alto project might combine incentives, using the amounts published on the City of Palo Alto Rebate Hub. A homeowner replaces an aging gas furnace and central air conditioner with a ducted heat pump. The project qualifies for the $2,500 Heat Pump HVAC rebate. Their 100-amp panel is tight on capacity, so they add a circuit splitter instead of upgrading the whole panel, which qualifies for a $500 add-on rebate. If the same household also replaces a gas water heater with a heat pump water heater, that is a separate core rebate with its own application.

Palo Alto Utility Rates Rose 8% in July. Gas Rose Fastest.
City Council approved an 8% overall utility increase for the fiscal year starting July 1, 2026. Gas went up twice as much as electricity.By the ComfortFlow teamJune 15, 2026
Call 650-460-3483

On June 15, 2026, the Palo Alto City Council approved an 8% overall utility rate increase for the fiscal year starting July 1, 2026: wastewater 16%, gas 9%, water 8%, electric 4.5% and refuse 3%. The City estimated the change at about $35 per month for the median household, including $7.30 for gas and $4.00 for electricity.
What changed
The City of Palo Alto’s June 2026 bill insert listed the proposed changes, and the Palo Alto Daily Post reported that City Council approved them on June 15, 2026.
Gas rose about twice as fast as electricity in Palo Alto’s July 2026 rate change. UtilityIncreaseMedian monthly change

The City’s gas estimate holds commodity prices constant; actual gas commodity rates change monthly.
What the July 2026 rate change means for a typical Palo Alto household. The longer trend
In April 2026, the Daily Post reported City projections that the average utility bill could rise from $441.50 to about $615.70 per month by 2031. The same report noted that the City transfers 18% of gas revenue to the general fund, and that utilities staff are studying a transition away from gas while still maintaining the gas system.
What it means for heating and cooling
Gas heat costs more each year. With gas rising faster than electricity, furnaces and gas water heaters get more expensive to run relative to heat pumps.
Palo Alto’s electricity is carbon neutral, so a heat pump cuts both cost exposure and emissions.
Rebates offset the upfront cost. CPAU’s Heat Pump HVAC rebate is $2,500, or $5,000 for income-eligible households, when a heat pump replaces gas heat.

Run the numbers for your home with our heat pump cost guide, or see heat pump installation.
A century of city-run gas
Palo Alto has distributed natural gas since 1917, and in October 2022 the City Council set a goal of carbon-neutral gas by 2030. Gas has been carbon neutral through offsets since July 1, 2017, but gas emissions in 2024 were only 34.5% below 1990, far behind the city’s overall progress.

There is no question in home heating that generates more arguments than this one. Scroll through any HVAC forum, neighborhood Facebook group, or Reddit thread and you will find homeowners locked in heated debate about whether a heat pump or a gas furnace is the smarter buy. Both sides have passionate defenders. Both sides cherry-pick numbers. And most of the time, neither side gives you the full picture.
That changes here. This article lays out the real numbers for 2026 - equipment costs, operating costs, federal tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act, maintenance, lifespan, and 10-year total cost of ownership. We are not going to tell you which one is "better" in some abstract sense, because the answer genuinely depends on where you live, what you pay for electricity and gas, and what your home looks like. But we are going to give you everything you need to figure it out for yourself.
No sales pitch. Just math.
How Each System Actually Works (30-Second Version)
Before comparing costs, it helps to understand the fundamental difference between these two machines. They solve the same problem - making your house warm - but they do it in completely different ways.
Gas Furnace
A gas furnace burns natural gas inside a combustion chamber. The hot gases pass through a metal heat exchanger, which warms the air that gets blown through your ductwork. The exhaust gases vent outside through a flue. It is a straightforward process: burn fuel, capture heat, distribute it. A furnace's efficiency is measured by AFUE (Annual Fuel Utilization Efficiency). A 96% AFUE furnace converts 96 cents of every dollar of gas into usable heat. The other 4 cents goes up the flue.
Heat Pump
A heat pump does not burn anything. It works like an air conditioner running in reverse - it extracts heat energy from the outdoor air and moves it inside. Even cold air contains thermal energy (anything above absolute zero, roughly -460°F, has heat in it). The heat pump chills its refrigerant to a temperature colder than the outdoor air, absorbs heat into that refrigerant, then compresses it to raise the temperature high enough to warm your home. In summer, it reverses direction and works as a standard air conditioner.
A heat pump's heating efficiency is measured by HSPF2 (Heating Seasonal Performance Factor), which captures performance across an entire heating season. The higher the number, the more heat you get per unit of electricity. You will also see COP (Coefficient of Performance) used to describe efficiency at a specific outdoor temperature.
The key difference in one sentence: A gas furnace creates heat by burning fuel. A heat pump moves heat that already exists in the outdoor air. Because moving heat takes less energy than creating it, heat pumps can deliver 2 to 4 times more heating energy than the electricity they consume. That is a thermodynamic advantage no combustion system can match.
------
Upfront Equipment and Installation Cost
Let's start with the number everyone asks about first: what does it cost to buy and install each system? These ranges come from aggregated contractor pricing data and reflect typical installations in 2025 and 2026. Your actual cost will vary based on system size, brand, ductwork condition, and local labor rates.

HOME HEATING · PALO ALTO, CA · 2026

Choose the heat pump: it heats and cools, and Palo Alto pays you to switch

Palo Alto's mild winters suit heat pumps. City rebates and rising gas rates favor one too. A furnace only wins if you're keeping a working AC and want the lowest cost this year.

Verdict: heat pump. A ducted heat pump replaces both furnace and AC. CPAU's rebate is $2,500 (standard), and gas rates are rising faster than electric. The federal tax credit is gone, so the city rebate is your main incentive.

Part 1

Upfront cost

Palo Alto winters rarely drop much below freezing, so the heat pump runs near its best efficiency most of the season. You don't need a cold-climate model or backup gas. Look for variable-speed (inverter) units with HSPF2 of about 9 or higher.

Part 3

Operating cost

Rule of thumb from the sources: if your electricity price per kWh is under about 3.5× your gas price per therm, a heat pump usually costs less to run. Above about 5×, a furnace can be cheaper in the coldest months. I couldn't pull the current CPAU per-kWh and per-therm rates, so check your latest bill for both numbers.

  • CPAU raised gas 9% and electric 4.5% on July 1, 2026.
  • The City projects the average utility bill rising from $441.50 to about $615.70 a month by 2031, and is studying a move away from gas.
  • Palo Alto electricity is carbon neutral, so a heat pump also cuts emissions.

A national modeled 10-year comparison puts a heat pump around $8,500 below furnace plus AC (about $22,500 vs $31,000, 2,000 sq ft, moderate climate). That model assumed the federal credit, so after removing the $2,000 credit and adding the CPAU rebate, the gap is roughly similar. Treat it as an estimate, not a Palo Alto quote.

  • Missing the 90-day deadline forfeits the rebate.

Use a CPAU Instant Rebate Partner and the rebate comes off your invoice. Apply for a reservation first, because the city typically approves in about 5 business days.

Part 5

When a furnace still makes sense

Heat pump wins if…

  • Your AC is old or you want cooling

  2. Get 2–3 quotes, including one from a CPAU Instant Rebate Partner, and ask for a load calculation.
  3. Ask about your panel and whether a circuit splitter avoids an upgrade.
  4. Reserve the rebate before installing, pass final inspection, and apply within 90 days.
  5. Ask about replacing the water heater in the same project.

Last updated: October 27, 2026
Last Updated: October 2026 | Region: Lake Tahoe (CA & NV)
Lake Tahoe in November 2026 includes a quiet shoulder season before ski resorts open, with some seasonal businesses closed. Resort openings usually start mid to late November.
Best For: November visitors
Shore & Base Elevation: Lake surface is about 6,225 ft; fall nights often drop near freezing by late October.
Season & Operating Window: Fall runs from September through early November, with aspen color usually peaking in early to mid October.
Pricing & Pass Access: Fall is shoulder season, so lodging often costs less than summer or ski season.
Parking & Reservations: Parking is easier than summer, but popular trailheads and event lots still fill on weekends.
Where to Stay Nearby: Compare Lake Tahoe lodging on Booking.com

Quick Answer: Many Forest Service beaches, campgrounds, restrooms, and parking areas close for winter between October and November, but national forest land remains open for walk-in recreation. Vikingsholm tours ended September 30, and Heavenly’s winter operations are scheduled to begin November 20, 2026. Sand Harbor’s visitor center is open year-round, while cruises such as the Spirit of Tahoe and M.S. Dixie II continue in November, weather and schedules permitting.

November is one of those in-between months at Lake Tahoe. Summer services have mostly wound down, but the ski season may not be fully underway yet. You can still enjoy the lake, trails, scenic drives, towns, and cruises, but you need to check which facilities are operating before you leave your hotel.
The most important thing to remember is that a closed parking lot, restroom, or campground does not always mean the surrounding public land is closed.
The Forest Service says national forest land remains open year-round, although winter parking is limited and services such as water, restrooms, and trash collection may not be available.

url: https://sierrarecmagazine.com/lake-tahoe-ski-resort-opening-dates-2026-27/

Winter just sent its first postcard. On Monday, October 12, the season’s first snow dusted the peaks around Lake Tahoe — Sierra-at-Tahoe reported measurable snowfall, and a light coating settled above 6,000 feet at Kirkwood, Heavenly and across the Sierra crest. OpenSnow’s Tahoe forecast called it the first dusting of the season, and at least one resort didn’t waste a minute of it.

Mt. Rose fires the snow guns first — again
Mt. Rose Ski Tahoe fired up its snowmaking system in the early hours of October 12, making it the first resort in Tahoe — and one of the first in the country — to make snow for the 2026–27 season. With Tahoe’s highest base elevation at 8,260 feet and mostly north- and east-facing slopes, Mt. Rose has opened first in Tahoe for four straight seasons, and it’s aiming to make it five: the resort is targeting a Friday, November 6 opening, weather and conditions permitting.
“It’s always exciting to see the first taste of winter, and as an added bonus, to be able to crank out snowmaking in force over the next couple of days,” said Mt. Rose marketing director Mike Pierce. Crews are building the base on the Lakeview Express and Kit Carson Bowl side first, and the resort opens once a signature intermediate trail carries a 10–14 inch base over at least 1,000 feet of vertical.
Heavenly used the same cold snap to test its snow guns and get the system dialed for the season — a good sign with its opening day just five weeks out.
All dates are announced targets, weather and conditions permitting:
Mt. Rose Ski Tahoe — Friday, November 6
Heavenly Mountain Resort — Friday, November 20
Northstar California — Friday, November 20
Palisades Tahoe — Wednesday, November 25 (the day before Thanksgiving)
Sugar Bowl — Friday, November 27
Diamond Peak — Thursday, December 3
Kirkwood — Friday, December 4

Sierra-at-Tahoe hasn’t posted its date yet — but after picking up the week’s only measurable snowfall, expect it in the mix soon. And just south of Tahoe, Mammoth Mountain is set for Friday, November 13.
A winter worth watching
If the forecasters are right, these dates are just the warm-up: a strong El Niño is expected to line up storm after storm for the Sierra this winter, a sharp reversal from last season’s short, dry year. The early cold snap is expected to soften this week, so this first dusting won’t all survive — but the guns are on, the calendar is set, and the countdown to first chair is officially running.
Planning your season? Explore our Lake Tahoe guides and winter coverage at Sierra Rec Magazine, and check back — we’ll update this post as more resorts post their dates.
Sources: Reno Gazette Journal (Oct. 12), POWDER (Oct. 13), OpenSnow Tahoe Daily Snow (Oct. 13), resort announcements via Vail Resorts and Ikon Pass.

Last updated: October 27, 2026
Last Updated: October 2026 | Region: Lake Tahoe (CA & NV)
Lake Tahoe in November 2026 includes a quiet shoulder season before ski resorts open, with some seasonal businesses closed. Resort openings usually start mid to late November.
Best For: November visitors
Shore & Base Elevation: Lake surface is about 6,225 ft; fall nights often drop near freezing by late October.
Season & Operating Window: Fall runs from September through early November, with aspen color usually peaking in early to mid October.
Pricing & Pass Access: Fall is shoulder season, so lodging often costs less than summer or ski season.
Parking & Reservations: Parking is easier than summer, but popular trailheads and event lots still fill on weekends.
Where to Stay Nearby: Compare Lake Tahoe lodging on Booking.com

Quick Answer: Many Forest Service beaches, campgrounds, restrooms, and parking areas close for winter between October and November, but national forest land remains open for walk-in recreation. Vikingsholm tours ended September 30, and Heavenly’s winter operations are scheduled to begin November 20, 2026. Sand Harbor’s visitor center is open year-round, while cruises such as the Spirit of Tahoe and M.S. Dixie II continue in November, weather and schedules permitting.

November is one of those in-between months at Lake Tahoe. Summer services have mostly wound down, but the ski season may not be fully underway yet. You can still enjoy the lake, trails, scenic drives, towns, and cruises, but you need to check which facilities are operating before you leave your hotel.
The most important thing to remember is that a closed parking lot, restroom, or campground does not always mean the surrounding public land is closed.
The Forest Service says national forest land remains open year-round, although winter parking is limited and services such as water, restrooms, and trash collection may not be available.
Last checked: October 22, 2026. Forest Service dates can change because of weather and site conditions.

Your trip is planned for Fri–Sun, Nov 6–8, and the stays, weather and day-by-day cards are above. I searched 2 nights (Nov 6–8) in South Lake Tahoe, so tell me if you want a third night added.

- **Stay:** Bally's ($63/night) and Golden Nugget ($70/night) are the cheapest. For something nicer, the Airbnb beachfront condo ($179/night, 4.92★) has hot tubs and a sauna.
- **Weather:** All three days are overcast with a low chance of rain. Nights get down to about 29°F and Saturday and Sunday afternoons reach about 54°F. Pack layers and shoes with good traction.
- **What's open:** Heavenly's ski season doesn't start until Nov 20, so this is a lake-and-trails trip. Vikingsholm tours have ended for the season, and its steep trail may be icy.
